name: Vase 'Colora' designed by Vicke Lindstrand
description:
A striking example of mid-century Scandinavian artistry, this “Colora” vase by Vicke Lindstrand (1904–1983)represents the timeless elegance of Swedish glass design. Handcrafted at Kosta glassworks and signed KOSTA 41673, this sculptural piece features deep blue undertones encapsulated within clear crystal glass, creating a fluid, organic interplay of light and color.

Lindstrand’s work at Kosta (1950–1973) marked one of the most celebrated eras in Swedish glass history. Known as Kostavicke, this period defined the essence of Scandinavian modernism, with softly sculptural forms, playful graphic lines, and a deep connection to natural elements. Each piece from this era reflects his mastery of form and color, qualities that made him a central figure in 20th-century Nordic design.

Renowned for his earlier creative phases Orreicke, Keramikvicke and Kostavicke, Lindstrand’s legacy continues to captivate collectors worldwide. His designs, from the iconic engraved vases The Pearl Fisherman and The Shark Killer to experimental color-layered works like the “Colora” series, remain highly sought after at international auctions.

This vase stands as a museum-quality example of Swedish art glass, perfect for discerning collectors and admirers of modern design.

Signed KOSTA 41673.

name: Vase 'Terra' designed by Monica Backström for Kosta Boda
description:
This vase from Monica Backström’s Terra series takes its inspiration from the irregular forms and surfaces of the natural world. Its softly asymmetric, almost planetary form is enveloped in deep midnight-blue glass, with a finely mottled surface that shifts between blue, grey and metallic tones as it catches the light. The highly polished exterior contrasts with the mineral-like interior colouring, giving the piece a sense of depth and weight that recalls a polished stone or fragment of volcanic rock.

Monica Backström (1939–2020) was one of the most distinctive figures in modern Swedish glass. During her long career at Kosta, she developed an experimental approach to glass that drew extensively on nature, the human body and the cosmos, often pushing the material towards unusual textures, colours and sculptural forms. Her work is represented in major collections including the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London and the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam.

Signed

name: Vase 'Höst' designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Kosta
description:
Designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Kosta in the 1960s, the Höst vase, meaning “Autumn” in English, is a refined example of Swedish art glass. The composition depicts dark, branching tree forms suspended within a thick body of clear glass, punctuated by small fragments of red, green, yellow and orange that evoke scattered autumn leaves.

The vase was produced using the demanding underfång, or cased glass, technique. Coloured elements and the black linear decoration are embedded beneath an outer layer of clear crystal, creating a remarkable sense of depth while keeping the various motifs sharply defined. The result is almost three-dimensional, with the trees appearing to float within the vessel rather than simply sitting on its surface.

Vicke Lindstrand was one of the most influential figures in twentieth-century Swedish glass design. After working at Orrefors from 1928 to 1941 and later serving as artistic director at Upsala-Ekeby, he joined Kosta in 1950, remaining there until 1973. During this period, Lindstrand played an important role in moving the factory towards a more experimental and expressive approach to glass, exploring bold colour, sculptural form and increasingly complex decorative techniques.

Marked LH 1754.

name: Vase designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Kosta
description:
A hand-blown glass vase designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Kosta in the 1950s, signed “LH 1131 / 62 HD”. The vase has a teardrop-shaped body raised on a clear glass foot, with an opaque white inner layer enclosed within the transparent outer glass.

Vicke Lindstrand’s years at Kosta, from 1950 to 1973, were among the most important periods in Swedish glass production. Often associated with the name “Kostavicke”, his work from this time combined sculptural forms, controlled colour and a strong sense of experimentation within traditional glassblowing. Lindstrand became one of the central figures of twentieth-century Nordic glass, bringing a more expressive and modern character to the medium.

Signed "LH 1131 / 62 HD"

name: Vase 'Savoy', model 3030, designed by Alvar Aalto for Iittala
description:
The Savoy vase was designed by Alvar Aalto in 1936 and produced by Ittalia. Formed in clear glass, the vase is defined by its free, undulating outline, created through a demanding glassblowing process in which the molten glass is shaped within a wooden mould. Each example carries subtle variations that reflect the hand-crafted nature of its production.

The design was originally developed for a glass competition organised by Iittala and later gained its name after being selected for the interior of Helsinki’s Savoy Hotel designed by Aalto and his wife Aino. The vase marked a departure from rigid geometric forms, introducing a more organic design rooted in landscape, water, and natural movement.

Alvar Aalto was a central figure in Finnish modernism, known for integrating architecture, furniture, and objects into a unified human-centred vision. The Savoy vase remains one of his most enduring designs.

Signed ALVAR AALTO- 3030

name: Vase 'Fiskgraal' designed by Edward Hald for Orrefors
description:
Edward Hald (1883–1980) was a central figure in the development of Swedish art glass through his long collaboration with Orrefors. His 'Fiskgraal' series is among his most celebrated works, created using the demanding Graal technique in which engraved motifs are encased within multiple layers of glass. The recurring fish and plant forms appear suspended in depth, a result of the complex layering and careful control of the blowing process, ensuring that each vase or bowl is unique.

These works exemplify Hald’s ability to unite technical mastery with artistic sensitivity. Drawing on his background in painting and ceramics, and influenced by his studies in Paris, Hald brought a distinctly modern, nature-inspired vocabulary to glass. The Fiskgraal series stands as an important contribution to Swedish Modern glass and remains highly regarded for its refinement, individuality, and craftsmanship.

Signed Orefors Graal Nr. 210 - E7 Edward Hald

name: Vase ‘Fiskgraal’ designed by Edward Hald for Orrefors
description:
Edward Hald (1883–1980) was a Swedish artist and designer known for his work with glass at Orrefors. One of his most recognised contributions is the Fiskgraal (Fish Graal) series, which demonstrates his skill in the Graal technique. This process involves layering and engraving glass to create detailed compositions. The fish and plant motifs have a sense of depth, achieved through multiple layers of glass. As each piece is individually blown and shaped, no two Fiskgraal vases or bowls are exactly alike.

The Fiskgraal series reflects Swedish glass craftsmanship and remains of interest to collectors. It was an advancement in glass design, combining technical precision with artistic expression.

Hald contributed to the development of Swedish Modern glass and helped bring international recognition to Orrefors. Born in Stockholm, he initially studied painting and ceramics before training under artists such as Henri Matisse in Paris. His transition into glass design led to a career in which he often depicted nature—fish, plants, and abstract patterns—within glass.

Signed.

name: Vase designed by Per B. Sundberg for Orrefors
description:
Produced during Sundberg’s collaboration with the Swedish glassworks Orrefors, this cylindrical vase from 2003 reflects his interest in surface as both structure and visual language. The vertical black lines, irregular in spacing and thickness, wrap around the white glass body in a rhythm that recalls hand-drawn marks or abstracted script. While minimalist in palette, the piece resists uniformity—emphasising variation and gesture over mechanical repetition. As in much of Sundberg’s glass work, form is restrained, allowing surface treatment to drive the visual character. The decoration appears to shift when viewed from different angles, reinforcing a sense of movement within the otherwise still form.

Signed.

name: Vase ‘Fish Graal’ designed by Edward Hald for Orrefors
description:
Edward Hald (1883 – 1980) is one of the well-known Swedish glass artists who have worked for Orrefors. After studying in Leipzig, he completed his artistic training with Henri Matisse in Paris. The famous Graal glass is one of the first masterpieces of Edward Hald, which he developed together with Simon Gate and Knut Bergqvist. In the 1920s, his work coined the term 'Swedish grace', the Swedish variant of Art Deco. The celestial globe that Edward Hald created for the 1930 Stockholm World's Fair is seen as the pinnacle of his career. During the Second World War he led the management of Orrefors, which forced him to perform a balancing act between economics and art.

The Graal glass technique was invented at Orrefors Glasbruk in Sweden, in 1916. In simple terms, the glassmakers create a piece with different coloured layers of glass, allow it to cool, then cut a design in one of the coloured layers to create a pattern. Then they re-heat it and case it with more crystal, and expand it. Obviously, this is a very complex, time-consuming process. The more complex the process, the more likely are errors and the more likely is the creation of pieces which can't be sold, even though hours of time have been invested in them.

A variation of the Graal technique is Fishgraal, invented by Edvard Hald in the 1930s. A design is painted on the glass, a green layer in this case, with liquid bitumen. Then, all the green layer which isn't covered with the pattern is acid-etched away, so that the pattern stands out on a clear background. Then it is reheated to 400-500 degrees Celcius and carefully covered with another thick layer of crystal. The name, Fishgraal, comes from the fact that the first collection featured fish. The designs are more detailed and the piece is not expanded, as they are in other forms of graal, so the designs are not distorted.

Signed.

name: Vase 'Fabula' designed by Per B. Sundberg for Orrefors
description:
Per B. Sundberg, a key figure in contemporary Swedish glass, developed the Fabula vases at Orrefors, the historic Swedish manufacturer. Reinterpreting Orrefors’ iconic Graal technique, Sundberg applies heat-resistant decals to a glass cylinder, which is then encased in clear crystal, reheated, and mouth-blown into form. While still hot, the object is further shaped using metal tools. Each Fabula vase is a unique piece.

Sundberg favours eclectic imagery, botanical engravings, comic-strip panels, elements of fauna and flora, and popular figures, combined in deliberately unexpected ways. He frequently works with discarded materials, notably vintage decals from the Gustavsberg porcelain manufactory. This approach functions as a form of narrative collage and creative recycling, infusing Orrefors glass with a pop, subtly ironic, and distinctly contemporary sensibility.

Signed.

name: Vase designed by Erik Höglund for Boda
description:
Erik Höglund started working for Boda when the company and the entire Swedish glass industry were expanding. As the world of glass was completely new to him, he wanted to learn as quickly as possible. So as not to disturb anyone at the glass furnace, he learned to blow and grind glass at night. Erik often stressed hard work as the key to success.

In 1954, Erik set out on his first scholarship abroad to Italy and Greece. He was more interested in sensuous Etruscan and Greco-Cretan culture than in classic lines and shapes. During the trip, he saw what real poverty was like, and his experiences in the war-torn lands of the Mediterranean made a strong impression on him.

Erik Höglund developed his own distinctive style in the 1950s. The shapes were simple and primordial, often inspired by primitive culture and folksy glass art. The objects were heavy and rustic, without sharp edges or flat surfaces. The glass often took human and sculptural shapes. Erik used coloured glass that was widely enhanced against the light. Air bubbles were present in the glass mass, sometimes induced by the production. He often stamped seals in the glass portraying faces, bulls, and other symbols. His artistic expression was one of conscious non-perfectionism. Therefore, Erik stood apart from the extremely successful Swedish glass art from the first part of the 20th century.

In 1957, Höglund received what was perhaps the most prestigious design award in the world, the Danish Lunning Prize. Soon enough, the sales of his glass designs skyrocketed Erik’s sense of design was to noticeably alter the daily life of the Swedish homes.

Signed.
